s01_open__b1.heard: Every second, software makes thousands of small decisions.

s01_open__b2.heard: Which team should get this ticket? Is this prompt a jailbreak? How urgent is this email?

s01_open__b3.heard: None of these are open questions. Each has a small, known set of answers, and that shape of problem deserves its own kind of model.

s01_open__b4.heard: Meet System 1 decision engines. Models that answer typed questions in a single forward pass, with a probability for every allowed answer.

s01_open__b5.heard: Our reference implementation is Laya, an open -source, multilingual decision engine.

s02_problem__b1.heard: Today, the default is to ask a large language model.

s02_problem__b2.heard: It writes the answer one token at a time. Then your code parses the text, checks the label is one you allowed, and retries when it isn't.

s02_problem__b3.heard: A full generation, a parser and a retry path, for a decision with only three possible answers.

s03_fastslow__b1.heard: The name comes from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow, which describes two modes of thought.

s03_fastslow__b2.heard: System 1 is fast, automatic and cheap, recognizing a face, sensing that a sentence is hostile.

s03_fastslow__b3.heard: System 2 is slow, deliberate and expensive, long multiplication, checking an argument.

s03_fastslow__b4.heard: Software has the same split. Language models made System 2 cheap enough to use everywhere, but most production decisions are still System 1 work. Known options, on every request, where speed and consistency matter most.

s03_fastslow__b5.heard: So the fast system should answer first, and its confidence should decide when to call in the slow one.

s04_arnar__b2.heard: An autoregressive model generates its answer token by token. Each token is another sequential forward pass, and the output can be malformed, or a label you never offered.

s04_arnar__b3.heard: A decision engine never writes the label. The options are part of its input. One forward pass scores every option side by side, and a softmax turns those scores into a distribution over exactly those options.

s04_arnar__b4.heard: So the answer is always valid. Every option gets a probability, so you see how close the runner -up was. And the cost doesn't depend on the answer.

s05_primitives__b1.heard: Every decision is expressed with three question types.

s05_primitives__b2.heard: Choice picks one label from several, like which department should handle a request. The label descriptions are what the model actually matches against.

s05_primitives__b3.heard: Score places the input on an ordered scale, like urgency, and returns the expected level, a probability -weighted average of the levels.

s05_primitives__b4.heard: And null returns the probability that a statement is true. Is this phishing? Does the user threaten to cancel?

s05_primitives__b5.heard: Several questions about the same input are answered together, in one batched call.

s06_sequence__b1.heard: Inside, each question becomes one row of tokens.

s06_sequence__b2.heard: A header with the question type and instructions. Then every option, each preceded by a mask token that marks where its score will be read. Then the input itself.

s06_sequence__b3.heard: The encoder is bidirectional, so each marker sees its option, the question, the rival options and the input, all at once.

s06_sequence__b4.heard: But the options share one fixed token budget. With seventy -seven options, each label keeps about three tokens, and similar labels collapse into the same text. The rule of thumb keep choice questions under about twenty options.

s07_forward__b1.heard: Now follow that row through the model.

s07_forward__b2.heard: A pretrained encoder, ModernBERT large for English, reads the whole row. A type embedding says which primitive this is, and a small two -layer decision head refines every position.

s07_forward__b3.heard: The model gathers the hidden vector at each marker, and a shared scorer turns each one into a single number, one logit per option.

s07_forward__b4.heard: Because options are inputs, not fixed output units, the same weights can score two options or twenty, even labels the model has never seen.

s07_forward__b5.heard: On a Tesla T4, one question takes about thirty -three milliseconds on the multilingual checkpoint. Ten questions take seventy -two, about seven milliseconds each.

s08_decoding__b1.heard: Decoding is a few lines. Divide the logits by a temperature, then apply a softmax.

s08_decoding__b2.heard: Temperature never changes which option wins. It only changes how confident the model sounds.

s08_decoding__b3.heard: And of the two confidence numbers the engine reports, gate on answer confidence, the probability of the chosen answer. That's the number calibration is fitted on.

s09_scoring__b1.heard: For those probabilities to mean anything, honesty has to be trained in.

s09_scoring__b2.heard: The tool is a strictly proper scoring rule, a reward that is maximized, on average, only by reporting what you truly believe.

s09_scoring__b3.heard: If the truth is seventy percent, the log, spherical and Brier scores all peak at exactly seventy. A linear reward keeps climbing towards certainty. It pays for overconfidence. And plain accuracy can't tell fifty -one percent from ninety -nine.

s10_rlcd__b1.heard: Laya's training method builds on this. It's called RLCD, Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.

s10_rlcd__b2.heard: For each item, it adds noise to the logits to sample a small group of candidate distributions, rewards each with a proper scoring rule, and compares it with its group's average.

s10_rlcd__b3.heard: The logits move towards the above -average samples, while a soft cross -entropy term pulls towards the teacher's full distribution, uncertainty included.

s10_rlcd__b4.heard: Fine -tuning is where the accuracy comes from. On the typed -decisions benchmark, the base model scores zero point three six. Fine -tuned, it reaches zero point seven seven, above the teacher's own self -agreement.

s11_calibration__b1.heard: A model is calibrated when its confidence means what it says, of the answers given at eighty percent, about eighty percent are right.

s11_calibration__b2.heard: The shipped checkpoints are over -confident. The fix is temperature scaling, fitted on held -out data. It never changes an answer, and it cuts calibration error from zero point four seven to zero point zero eight.

s11_calibration__b3.heard: But calibration can't rescue an input the model cannot read. On Khmer, the English checkpoint scored zero accuracy, at ninety -five percent confidence.

s12_router__b1.heard: That's why Laya ships three checkpoints and a router.

s12_router__b2.heard: One for English, a faster multilingual one for over a hundred languages, and one fine -tuned for four specific workflows.

s12_router__b3.heard: Before any forward pass, the router detects script and language in well under a millisecond, and sends the text to a checkpoint that can read it. Across fifty -one languages, usable coverage nearly doubles, from twenty -three to forty -five.

s13_production__b1.heard: In production, a decision engine returns evidence, not permission.

s13_production__b2.heard: The core pattern is confidence gating. Above a threshold, act automatically. Below it, escalate to a human, a rule, or a larger model. The threshold is a policy, chosen from measured accuracy and the cost of mistakes.

s13_production__b3.heard: Roll out in stages. Shadow, compare, choose a policy, then promote a bounded slice of traffic, with a rollback plan.

s14_agents__b2.heard: An agent loop is full of small, typed decisions. Is this input safe? Which tool comes next? Is the task done? Is this output good enough to send?

s14_agents__b3.heard: System 1 takes those in milliseconds, and hands only the uncertain cases to System 2.

s14_agents__b4.heard: In one browser agent, fine -tuning lifted the right -element choice from ten percent, which is chance, to nearly two thirds, with each step decided in about twenty milliseconds.

s15_limits__b1.heard: It isn't magic, and the limits deserve plain words.

s15_limits__b2.heard: A decision engine is not a reasoner, it can't explain itself or answer open questions. Zero -shot, the base checkpoints are near chance on specialized workflows, they ship over -confident, and long option lists or other languages need care.

s15_limits__b3.heard: So evaluate on your own traffic, fine -tune on your own decisions, fit temperatures on held -out data, and gate every change in CI.

s16_outro__b1.heard: Let System 1 answer first, in one pass, with honest probabilities.

s16_outro__b2.heard: And let calibrated confidence decide when it's time to think slow.

s16_outro__b3.heard: That's System 1 decision engines. Explore all eighteen chapters in the interactive tutorial.
